extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (also patent prosecutors and patent attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting patent claim terms during examination using the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) standard, including plain-meaning rules, lexicography, disavowal, means-plus-function, and when to consult extrinsic evidence. Focused on claim construction practices applicable in prosecution before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, the pending claims must be 'given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is the standard the USPTO applies in prosecution (citing Phillips, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., etc.). It is applied to the words of the proposed claims as they would be understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account definitions or other enlightenment in the written description. BRI is used because applicants can amend claims during prosecution; giving claims their BRI reduces the possibility that an issued claim will be later interpreted more broadly than justified. The Office does not interpret claims during prosecution the same way courts do in infringement or validity proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI is not the broadest possible interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation does not mean the broadest possible interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The meaning given to a claim term must be consistent with the ordinary and customary meaning of the term (unless specially defined), and consistent with the use of the term in the specification and drawings. The BRI must also be consistent with the interpretation those skilled in the art would reach (citing In re Cortright, Buszard examples). Examiners should avoid unreasonable constructions that are inconsistent with the disclosure or ordinary meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain meaning rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of a claim must be given their 'plain meaning' unless such meaning is inconsistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Plain meaning’ = the ordinary and customary meaning given by those of ordinary skill in the art at the relevant time (effective filing date). The best source is the specification (serves as a glossary when clear). Other intrinsic sources include the claims themselves, drawings, and prosecution history. Ordinary words whose meaning is clear are construed to mean exactly what they say unless context indicates otherwise (examples: heating dough vs oven air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to import into a claim limitations that are not part of the claim simply because they appear in the written description or preferred embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A particular embodiment in the specification should not be read into a claim when the claim language is broader than the embodiment (citing Superguide, Liebel‑Flarsheim, E‑Pass). Examiners should refrain from narrowing claims by reading disclosed embodiments or exemplary sequences into the claim unless the claim language itself demands it or a statutory provision (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 112(f)) requires reference to the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer intrinsic evidence; use extrinsic evidence only when intrinsic is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary and customary meaning should be derived from intrinsic evidence (claims, specification, drawings); extrinsic evidence (dictionaries, treatises, expert testimony) is secondary and used only if intrinsic evidence fails to provide sufficient clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification is clear about scope and content, there's no need to consult extrinsic evidence (citing 3M v. Tredegar). In some cases where claims, specification, and prosecution history do not offer sufficient clarity, extrinsic evidence may be necessary (Actelion example). Any meaning taken from prior art or dictionaries must be consistent with the specification and drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant-as-lexicographer (special definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a term in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To act as their own lexicographer the applicant must define the term with reasonable clarity, deliberateness, and precision in the specification so that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand the departure from common usage (citing In re Paulsen, Intellicall). When an explicit definition is provided, that definition controls claim interpretation (Toro Co. v. White). Any special meaning must be sufficiently clear in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disavowal (clear and unmistakable disclaimer of claim scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may rebut ordinary meaning by clearly disavowing or disclaiming the full scope of a claim term in the specification; disavowal must be clear and unmistakable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification makes clear the invention does not include a particular feature, that feature is outside the reach of the claims even if the claim language appears broad (SciMed example). Disavowal can be explicit or, in some cases, implicit (e.g., specification repeatedly disparages a feature and all embodiments exclude it — In re Abbott Diabetes Care). If examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make that interpretation clear on the record and cite MPEP § 2173.05(a) as relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)) construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When an element is claimed using means- or step-plus-function language (112(f)/pre‑AIA 112 sixth paragraph), the specification must be consulted to determine the corresponding structure, material, or acts and the claimed element is limited to those structures/materials/acts and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function limitations are construed by reference to the specification (citing In re Donaldson and MPEP §§2181–2186). Examiners must identify the corresponding structure in the written description and construe the claim limitation accordingly; the limitation is not indefinite merely because the specification discloses only a single embodiment, but the corresponding structure must be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flow-chart process for determining claim term meaning (when 112(f) not invoked)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning, check the specification for a special definition; if none, apply the ordinary meaning. If no ordinary meaning exists, follow the alternative flow to seek a special definition or other guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MPEP flowchart directs examiners to: (1) determine whether the term has an ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art; (2) if so, check specification for a special definition — if present, use it (and acknowledge it in the Office action); (3) if not present, apply the ordinary meaning. If the term lacks ordinary meaning, consult the specification for an implied definition and, if necessary, other evidence. Office actions should acknowledge and identify any special definitions used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar, syntax, and ordinary reading of claim language control scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammatical and syntactic features of claim language (e.g., singular vs plural, antecedent basis) affect interpretation and may limit claim scope based on ordinary reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be read according to their grammar and ordinary usage: e.g., use of 'said microprocessor' can require a singular element capable of performing recited functions (Salazar example). Examiners should ensure antecedent basis and claim grammar are properly considered and addressed (see MPEP § 2173.05(e) and related examples).
